# Copilot Repository Instructions

- Write for the intended reader using plain language. Introduce unfamiliar terms with a short definition before using them in detailed explanations.
- Organize conceptual and architecture documents as “overall diagram and explanation → individual components.” State the purpose briefly, then explain the whole system before its parts. Use concrete examples within the relevant explanations rather than adding mandatory chapters.
- For each relevant component, explain its responsibility, implementation form, execution environment, inputs, and outputs. For customization mechanisms, identify who loads or invokes them and what happens next. Distinguish files, libraries, software roles, and running processes.
- Keep diagrams inside the Markdown document. Prefer fenced `mermaid` blocks for GitHub and ASCII trees for directories. Use fenced PlantUML only when the target viewer is known to support it; GitHub does not natively render PlantUML blocks.
- Architecture documents must not depend on PNGs, separate diagram source files, or generation scripts. Create image exports only when explicitly requested.
- Use focused diagrams to explain relationships, information flow, execution locations, and boundaries. Avoid decorative repetition. Give diagrams descriptive labels, explain how to read them, and check syntax, arrow direction, and consistency with the prose. Check rendering when possible and report unrun checks in the completion message.
- Prefer concise bullet points with one main idea per item; use short prose where it makes the explanation clearer.
- Keep diagrams consistent between English and Japanese versions; translate explanatory labels while preserving identifiers and behavior.

[日本語](copilot-instructions_jp.md)

- This is a personal repository for learning, experimentation, and development.
- The canonical shared rules are in [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md); read it when file access is available.
- Essential rules are repeated here so they do not depend on following a link.
- Keep this file aligned with that source.
- Japanese translations are reading aids, not separate instruction sources.
- Follow applicable host instructions and user requirements; report unresolved conflicts.

- Write authored documentation in English first and add a Japanese `_jp.md` translation beside it. Update both in the same commit and add reciprocal relative links. Preserve code, commands, paths, API names, identifiers, and machine-readable keys; translate prose without changing behavior. Keep meaning, structure, examples, and warnings consistent. English is canonical. Do not rename required configuration files or translate generated or third-party files just to create pairs.
- Every new application must include `README.md` and a matching `README_jp.md` in its own directory. Document its purpose, prerequisites, installation, startup commands, basic usage, and validation commands with expected results; include configuration instructions when configuration is required. Create or update both READMEs in the same change as the application and keep them current when setup, commands, or behavior changes. Application work is incomplete until both READMEs are present and up to date. Link them from the repository's root `README.md` and `README_jp.md` when adding an application.
- Create directories only when adding content. Do not add empty directories or `.gitkeep`. Organize study materials under `learning/` by topic; create `experiments/`, `projects/`, `notes/`, and `scripts/` only as needed.
- Use lowercase `snake_case` for new names, except conventional names, required configuration filenames, and existing names. Keep setup and validation instructions near their projects or experiments.
- Include purpose, explanations, examples, and references where useful, without empty boilerplate. Distinguish sourced facts, quotations, interpretations, and assumptions; cite borrowed material and respect licenses. Document prerequisites, commands, and expected results for runnable examples. Record experiment goals, environments, procedures, results, and interpretation, including benchmark conditions.
- Inspect existing files before editing, keep changes focused, and preserve unrelated user work. Add only necessary dependencies using existing package managers and lockfiles; avoid unrelated updates.
- Validate appropriately: check documentation formatting, relative links, and translation consistency; use relevant existing tests and builds for code. Report passed, failed, skipped, and unrun checks accurately.
- Never commit credentials, personal information, local-only configuration, dependency caches, or generated build outputs. Use secret-free configuration examples and maintain `.gitignore` as needed.
- Before starting or resuming each task, check the current branch and working tree, then run `git pull` with an explicit remote and the intended integration branch (the repository default unless specified otherwise) before editing files. For example, use `git pull --ff-only origin main` when a fast-forward is possible. Also synchronize the working branch's upstream when it exists, and reread any updated repository instructions after pulling.
- A missing upstream or failed pull does not count as synchronization. If an upstream was deleted, explicitly pull the intended integration branch. Preserve local changes and resolve conflicts safely; if synchronization remains blocked, report the blocker before starting edits. Do not reset or discard unrelated work to make a pull succeed.
- Use English commit messages and one purpose per commit. Write pull request titles and descriptions in English. After each completed change, validate it, commit it, and push to the working branch unless the user explicitly requests otherwise. Report the commit SHA and push result. After validation, commit, and a successful push, check for an open pull request for the working branch. If none exists and there are changes to propose, create a draft pull request targeting the intended integration branch (the repository default unless specified otherwise). If one exists, update its title and description to reflect the final changes and validation, preserving relevant existing context and review state. Avoid duplicate pull requests. Report the PR URL. Do not merge, enable auto-merge, publish releases, or deploy unless explicitly requested. If authentication or permissions prevent PR creation or updates, report the blocker without claiming success. Direct pushes to `main` and force pushes require explicit instructions. Do not reset or overwrite unrelated work.
